country.comment: The study analyzes 20 municipalities with headquarters in the Eastern Watersheds (Bacias Hidrográficas do Leste, BHL) in the State of Bahia, Brazil.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Title/Affiliations; PDF p. 4, Section 1; PDF p. 5–6, Section 1

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive quantitative and governance indicators only; no inferential statistical model, 95% confidence intervals, or p-values are reported. Note minor internal discrepancies in the paper: Table 1 lists 12 municipalities (with 'Uma' for Una) while text on PDF p. 20 states 13; Table 3 lists 4 non-responding municipalities while text on PDF p. 26 states 5.
effect_estimate.value: Descriptive analysis only (no regression point estimates, 95% CIs, or p-values reported). Across the 20 municipalities headquartered in Bahia's Bacias Hidrográficas do Leste (635,546 residents in 2017), 2017 sewage collection averaged 37.95% across 13 analyzed municipalities (vs. 54.65% Bahia state average; 4 municipalities had 0% collection), sewage treatment averaged 11.54% across 17 municipalities (vs. 50.42% state average; 70.58% had 0% treatment), and population sewage service coverage averaged 39.39% across the analyzed BHL population (537,298 residents, 84.54% of BHL; 4 municipalities at 0%). Per capita sewage investment in 2016–2017 was below R$ 0.20 in 10 of 12 analyzed municipalities (at least 50% of the 20 BHL municipalities), with only Ilhéus exceeding the state average in 2017 (R$ 42.63 per inhabitant). Regarding legal/governance mechanisms, 10 years after Law 11.445/2007 only 15% (3/20) of municipalities had completed a Municipal Basic Sanitation Plan (PMSB) by 2017, 40% (8/20) were drafting one, and 45% (9/20) had none, leaving 85% (17/20) ineligible for federal sanitation transfers starting in 2020 under Decree 9.254/2017. Only 35% (7/20) had complete 2016–2017 sewage data in SNIS; among the 13 municipalities sent Freedom of Information (LAI) requests, 69.23% (9/13) had an agency linked in e-SIC (4 required physical filing due to unlinked portals and 1 restricted online filing via a closed profession list), and 4–5 failed to respond within the statutory 20-day (+10-day) deadline.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 17–27, Section 3, Figures 1–4, Tables 1–3, and Quadro 1; PDF p. 28–29, Section 4

mechanism_certainty.comment: Ceiling is 2 under Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework. Coded as 1 because while the authors directly audit municipal PMSB status and e-SIC/LAI administrative barriers to researcher data requests, the relationship between these legal/governance mechanisms and actual household sanitation access/coverage in 2016–2017 is documented only through parallel descriptive municipal indicators (and the federal budget transfer cutoff for lacking a PMSB under Decree 9.254/2017 was prospective for 2020 rather than directly observed operating on 2016–2017 sanitation access).
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF p. 14–16, Section 2; PDF p. 17–27, Section 3, Tables 1–3 and Quadro 1

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines municipal sanitation planning mandates (PMSB under Law 11.445/2007 and Decree 7.217/2010), federal funding cutoff sanctions and repeated deadline postponements (Decrees 8.211/2014, 8.629/2015, 9.254/2017), STJ judicial review upholding sewage tariff collection without wastewater treatment (AgRg no REsp 1505229/PR), intergovernmental/intersectoral coordination, and citizen participation/social control via Freedom of Information (LAI / e-SIC) procedures, portal hurdles, and statutory response delays.

Note: e-SIC response delays/non-responses in Table 3 concern researcher freedom-of-information requests for aggregate SNIS data rather than household service connection applications.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Doctrinal-empirical / legal-institutional governance study combining statutory, regulatory, and judicial analysis of Brazilian sanitation and freedom-of-information law (Section 2) with descriptive municipal administrative indicators (SNIS, IBGE MUNIC) and a direct Freedom of Information (LAI / e-SIC) compliance audit across 20 municipalities, with no analytical regression or conventional qualitative interview/ethnographic component.

sample_size.comment: The BHL encompasses 24 municipalities overall, of which the 20 municipalities with municipal headquarters inside the watershed form the study sample; indicator-specific municipal counts vary between 12 and 20 due to missing SNIS/municipal records.
sample_size.value: 20 municipalities headquartered in the Bacias Hidrográficas do Leste (BHL), Bahia (total resident population of 635,546 inhabitants in 2017), observed across 2016–2017 (subsamples by indicator: n = 20 municipalities for PMSB governance and SNIS completeness; n = 17 for sewage treatment; n = 13 for sewage collection; n = 13 reported in text [12 listed in Table 1; 537,298 inhabitants] for population sewage coverage; n = 12 for per capita investment; n = 13 municipalities sent LAI/e-SIC information requests)
sample_size.where_found: PDF p. 3, Resumo; PDF p. 5–6, Section 1; PDF p. 17–27, Section 3, Figures 1–4, Tables 1–3, and Quadro 1

study_design.comment: Described by the authors as having a qualitative-quantitative ('quali-quantitativa') nature; operationalized as a legal-doctrinal analysis (Section 2) paired with descriptive municipal indicator analysis and a primary administrative transparency (LAI/e-SIC) audit (Section 3), without inferential statistical testing.
study_design.value: Legal-empirical and descriptive mixed-source ('quali-quantitativa') municipal governance study combining doctrinal legal analysis (Lei 11.445/2007, Decreto 7.217/2010, Lei 12.527/2011, and STJ case law) with descriptive analysis of secondary administrative data (SNIS and IBGE MUNIC, 2016–2017) and primary Freedom of Information (LAI) requests via e-SIC and physical mail
